Problem 3 (Engine block/head joint GP experiment). A 27-run experiment on eight factors $x_1, \dots, x_8$ (gasket thickness, contour zones, transition, bead profile, coining depth, deck flatness, load/deflection variation, head-bolt force variation), response gap lift $y$. Because `engine_experiment_data.txt` is not available, I cannot honestly report numerical MLEs, cross-validation errors, plots, or optimal factor settings. Below is the complete analysis I would perform from the data, using only likelihood evaluation, linear algebra, and numerical optimization—not a GP package.

Let the 27 runs be \((x_i,y_i)\), \(i=1,\dots,n\), \(n=27\), with \(x_i\in\mathbb R^8\). For a parameter vector \(\theta=(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_8)\), define

\[
R_\theta(i,j)
=
\exp\left\{-\sum_{k=1}^8 \theta_k(x_{ik}-x_{jk})^2\right\}.
\]

The covariance matrix is \(\sigma^2 R_\theta\).

---

## (1) Constant-mean GP: MLEs for \(\mu,\theta,\sigma^2\)

The model is

\[
Y(x)=\mu+Z(x),
\]

with

\[
Z\sim GP\{0,\sigma^2 R_\theta(\cdot,\cdot)\}.
\]

Let \(1_n=(1,\dots,1)^T\), \(y=(y_1,\dots,y_n)^T\), and \(R=R_\theta\).

For fixed \(\theta\), the log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\mu,\sigma^2,\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log\sigma^2
-\frac12\log |R_\theta|
-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}(y-\mu 1_n)^T R_\theta^{-1}(y-\mu 1_n).
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the generalized least squares MLE of \(\mu\) is

\[
\widehat\mu(\theta)
=
\frac{1_n^T R_\theta^{-1} y}{1_n^T R_\theta^{-1}1_n}.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
=
\frac1n
\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}^T
R_\theta^{-1}
\{y-\widehat\mu(\theta)1_n\}.
\]

The profile log-likelihood is therefore

\[
\ell_p(\theta)
=
-\frac n2\log(2\pi)
-\frac n2\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
-\frac12 \log |R_\theta|
-\frac n2.
\]

Equivalently, \(\widehat\theta\) minimizes

\[
\Psi(\theta)
=
n\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta_k\ge 0}
\left\{
n\log \widehat{\sigma}^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|
\right\},
\]

and then

\[
\widehat\mu=\widehat\mu(\widehat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat{\sigma}^2=\widehat{\sigma}^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

In practice I would optimize over \(\eta_k=\log \theta_k\) to enforce positivity, use a Cholesky factorization of \(R_\theta\), and use multiple starting values to avoid poor local optima. If some \(\widehat\theta_k\) is essentially zero, that factor is effectively inactive in the correlation.

Because the data file is missing, the numerical estimates \(\widehat\mu,\widehat\theta,\widehat\sigma^2\) cannot be reported.

---

## (2) BLUP and plug-in predictive distribution

Let \(x_0\) be a new input. Define

\[
r(x_0)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
R_\theta(x_0,x_1)\\
\vdots\\
R_\theta(x_0,x_n)
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For the constant-mean model, using the MLEs from part (1), the BLUP is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
\widehat\mu
+
r(x_0)^T R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-\widehat\mu 1_n\}.
\]

Let

\[
C=R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}.
\]

The plug-in predictive variance, accounting for estimation of the constant mean but not for uncertainty in \(\widehat\theta\) or \(\widehat\sigma^2\), is

\[
\widehat s^2(x_0)
=
\widehat\sigma^2
\left[
1
-
r(x_0)^T C r(x_0)
+
\frac{\{1-1_n^T C r(x_0)\}^2}{1_n^T C1_n}
\right].
\]

Thus the plug-in predictive distribution is

\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),
\widehat s^2(x_0)
\right).
\]

A 95% plug-in predictive interval is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)\pm 1.96\,\widehat s(x_0).
\]

---

## (3) Leave-one-out cross-validation prediction error for the constant-mean GP

For exact leave-one-out cross-validation, for each \(i=1,\dots,n\), I would remove observation \(i\), refit the model to the remaining \(n-1\) observations, compute the BLUP at \(x_i\), and define

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
y_i-\widehat y_{-i}(x_i).
\]

The leave-one-out mean squared prediction error is

\[
\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2,
\]

and the root mean squared prediction error is

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2
\right]^{1/2}.
\]

A useful scale-free measure is

\[
Q^2_{\text{LOO}}
=
1-
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2}
{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar y)^2}.
\]

If one fixes \(\theta=\widehat\theta\) from the full data set rather than refitting \(\theta\) for each deletion, the leave-one-out errors can be computed efficiently. Let

\[
C=R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1},
\]

and define the generalized residual precision matrix

\[
Q
=
C
-
C1_n(1_n^T C1_n)^{-1}1_n^T C.
\]

Then the leave-one-out prediction error is

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}},
\]

and hence

\[
\widehat y_{-i}(x_i)
=
y_i-\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

The corresponding LOO predictive variance is approximately

\[
\widehat s^2_{-i}
=
\frac{\widehat\sigma^2}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

The requested numerical cross-validation prediction error cannot be computed without the data file.

---

## (4) Linear trend GP using \(x_1\) and \(x_6\)

Now use the model

\[
Y(x)
=
\beta_0+x_1\beta_1+x_6\beta_2+Z(x),
\]

with the same squared exponential correlation.

Define the regression vector

\[
f(x)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_1\\
x_6
\end{pmatrix},
\]

and let

\[
F
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_{11} & x_{16}\\
1 & x_{21} & x_{26}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\
1 & x_{n1} & x_{n6}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the GLS MLE of \(\beta\) is

\[
\widehat\beta(\theta)
=
(F^T R_\theta^{-1}F)^{-1}
F^T R_\theta^{-1}y.
\]

The profile estimate of \(\sigma^2\) is

\[
\widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
=
\frac1n
\{y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\}^T
R_\theta^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\}.
\]

The profile log-likelihood is maximized, equivalently, by minimizing

\[
\Psi(\theta)
=
n\log \widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta_k\ge 0}
\left\{
n\log \widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|
\right\}.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat\beta=\widehat\beta(\widehat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat\sigma^2=\widehat\sigma^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

The BLUP at a new point \(x_0\) is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
f(x_0)^T\widehat\beta
+
r(x_0)^T
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta\}.
\]

Let

\[
C=R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}.
\]

The plug-in universal kriging predictive variance is

\[
\widehat s^2(x_0)
=
\widehat\sigma^2
\left[
1
-
r(x_0)^T C r(x_0)
+
q(x_0)^T
(F^T C F)^{-1}
q(x_0)
\right],
\]

where

\[
q(x_0)
=
f(x_0)-F^T C r(x_0).
\]

Thus

\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),
\widehat s^2(x_0)
\right).
\]

For leave-one-out cross-validation, the exact approach is again to refit the model with observation \(i\) omitted and predict \(y_i\). The LOO errors are

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
y_i-\widehat y_{-i}(x_i),
\]

and I would report

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
(e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2
\right]^{1/2}.
\]

If \(\theta\) is held fixed at its full-data estimate, define

\[
Q
=
C
-
CF(F^T CF)^{-1}F^T C.
\]

Then

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}},
\qquad
\widehat y_{-i}(x_i)
=
y_i-\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

Again, numerical values require the missing data file.

---

## (5) Final model comparison and recommendation rule

I would compare the constant-mean GP and the linear-trend GP using both likelihood-based and prediction-based criteria.

For the constant-mean model,

\[
k_0=1+8+1=10
\]

parameters: \(\mu\), eight \(\theta\)'s, and \(\sigma^2\).

For the linear-trend model,

\[
k_1=3+8+1=12
\]

parameters: \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2\), eight \(\theta\)'s, and \(\sigma^2\).

I would compute

\[
\operatorname{AIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\psi)+2k,
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{BIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\psi)+k\log n.
\]

Because \(n=27\) is small, I would emphasize out-of-sample predictive performance, especially

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}},
\qquad
\operatorname{MAE}_{\text{LOO}},
\qquad
Q^2_{\text{LOO}},
\]

and, if predictive variances are used,

\[
\operatorname{NLPD}
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
\frac12\log(2\pi \widehat s_{-i}^2)
+
\frac{(e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2}{2\widehat s_{-i}^2}
\right].
\]

A good probabilistic predictor should also have approximately calibrated standardized LOO errors,

\[
z_i
=
\frac{e_i^{\text{LOO}}}{\widehat s_{-i}},
\]

with empirical variance near one and no obvious trend against fitted values.

My model-selection rule would be:

- choose the linear-trend GP if it gives materially smaller LOO RMSE/MAE, larger \(Q^2_{\text{LOO}}\), smaller NLPD, and acceptable AIC/BIC;
- otherwise choose the simpler constant-mean GP.

Without the data, the final model cannot be selected numerically.

---

## (6) BLUP as a function of \(x_1\) with 95% predictive bands

Let the selected final model have regression vector \(f(x)\), estimated coefficients \(\widehat\beta\), covariance parameter \(\widehat\theta\), and variance estimate \(\widehat\sigma^2\).

To plot the fitted response as a function of \(x_1\), one must hold the other factors fixed. I would typically choose either

1. their nominal center values, or  
2. the estimated optimal values from part (7).

Let

\[
x(t)
=
(t,c_2,c_3,\dots,c_8),
\]

where \(t\) varies over the experimental range of \(x_1\) and \((c_2,\dots,c_8)\) are fixed.

For each grid value \(t\), compute

\[
\widehat m(t)
=
\widehat y\{x(t)\},
\]

and

\[
\widehat s^2(t)
=
\widehat s^2\{x(t)\}.
\]

Then plot

\[
t\mapsto \widehat m(t),
\]

with 95% plug-in predictive bands

\[
\widehat m(t)\pm 1.96\,\widehat s(t).
\]

The plot cannot be produced numerically without the data.

---

## (7) Optimization of the eight factor settings

For the final fitted model, the predicted mean response has the form

\[
\widehat m(x)
=
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
+
r(x)^T\widehat\alpha,
\]

where

\[
\widehat\alpha
=
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta\}.
\]

The goal is to solve

\[
\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}
=
\arg\min_{x\in \mathcal D}
\widehat m(x),
\]

where \(\mathcal D\) is the feasible region for the eight factors, usually the product of their experimental ranges.

Because \(\widehat m(x)\) is generally nonconvex, I would use a multistart global search followed by local optimization.

For continuous factors, the derivative is available analytically. Let

\[
r_j(x)
=
\exp\left\{
-\sum_{k=1}^8
\widehat\theta_k(x_k-x_{jk})^2
\right\}.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat m(x)
=
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
+
\sum_{j=1}^n
\widehat\alpha_j r_j(x).
\]

For coordinate \(k\),

\[
\frac{\partial \widehat m(x)}{\partial x_k}
=
\frac{\partial f(x)^T\widehat\beta}{\partial x_k}
-
2\widehat\theta_k
\sum_{j=1}^n
\widehat\alpha_j
r_j(x)(x_k-x_{jk}).
\]

For the linear-trend model,

\[
\frac{\partial f(x)^T\widehat\beta}{\partial x_k}
=
\begin{cases}
\widehat\beta_1, & k=1,\\
\widehat\beta_2, & k=6,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

The algorithm would be:

1. Scale all factors to their coded experimental ranges.
2. Generate many starting points in \(\mathcal D\), for example by Latin hypercube or Sobol sampling.
3. Evaluate \(\widehat m(x)\) at all starting points.
4. Keep the best several candidates.
5. From each candidate, run a bounded gradient-based optimizer such as L-BFGS-B using the gradient above.
6. Compare all local minima and choose the one with the smallest predicted gap lift.
7. Report \(\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}\), \(\widehat m(\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}})\), and the predictive standard error \(\widehat s(\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}})\).

If some factors are genuinely discrete rather than continuous, I would enumerate their possible levels and run the continuous optimization conditionally on each discrete combination.

The numerical optimum cannot be reported without the missing experiment file.

## (3) Leave-one-out cross-validation prediction error for the constant-mean GP

For exact leave-one-out cross-validation, for each \(i=1,\dots,n\), I would remove observation \(i\), refit the model to the remaining \(n-1\) observations, compute the BLUP at \(x_i\), and define

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
y_i-\widehat y_{-i}(x_i).
\]

The leave-one-out mean squared prediction error is

\[
\operatorname{MSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2,
\]

and the root mean squared prediction error is

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
\left(e_i^{\text{LOO}}\right)^2
\right]^{1/2}.
\]

A useful scale-free measure is

\[
Q^2_{\text{LOO}}
=
1-
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2}
{\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar y)^2}.
\]

If one fixes \(\theta=\widehat\theta\) from the full data set rather than refitting \(\theta\) for each deletion, the leave-one-out errors can be computed efficiently. Let

\[
C=R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1},
\]

and define the generalized residual precision matrix

\[
Q
=
C
-
C1_n(1_n^T C1_n)^{-1}1_n^T C.
\]

Then the leave-one-out prediction error is

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}},
\]

and hence

\[
\widehat y_{-i}(x_i)
=
y_i-\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

The corresponding LOO predictive variance is approximately

\[
\widehat s^2_{-i}
=
\frac{\widehat\sigma^2}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

The requested numerical cross-validation prediction error cannot be computed without the data file.

## (4) Linear trend GP using \(x_1\) and \(x_6\)

Now use the model

\[
Y(x)
=
\beta_0+x_1\beta_1+x_6\beta_2+Z(x),
\]

with the same squared exponential correlation.

Define the regression vector

\[
f(x)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_1\\
x_6
\end{pmatrix},
\]

and let

\[
F
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & x_{11} & x_{16}\\
1 & x_{21} & x_{26}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots\\
1 & x_{n1} & x_{n6}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

For fixed \(\theta\), the GLS MLE of \(\beta\) is

\[
\widehat\beta(\theta)
=
(F^T R_\theta^{-1}F)^{-1}
F^T R_\theta^{-1}y.
\]

The profile estimate of \(\sigma^2\) is

\[
\widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
=
\frac1n
\{y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\}^T
R_\theta^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta(\theta)\}.
\]

The profile log-likelihood is maximized, equivalently, by minimizing

\[
\Psi(\theta)
=
n\log \widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|.
\]

Thus

\[
\widehat\theta
=
\arg\min_{\theta_k\ge 0}
\left\{
n\log \widehat\sigma^2(\theta)
+
\log |R_\theta|
\right\}.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat\beta=\widehat\beta(\widehat\theta),
\qquad
\widehat\sigma^2=\widehat\sigma^2(\widehat\theta).
\]

The BLUP at a new point \(x_0\) is

\[
\widehat y(x_0)
=
f(x_0)^T\widehat\beta
+
r(x_0)^T
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta\}.
\]

Let

\[
C=R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}.
\]

The plug-in universal kriging predictive variance is

\[
\widehat s^2(x_0)
=
\widehat\sigma^2
\left[
1
-
r(x_0)^T C r(x_0)
+
q(x_0)^T
(F^T C F)^{-1}
q(x_0)
\right],
\]

where

\[
q(x_0)
=
f(x_0)-F^T C r(x_0).
\]

Thus

\[
Y(x_0)\mid y
\approx
N\left(
\widehat y(x_0),
\widehat s^2(x_0)
\right).
\]

For leave-one-out cross-validation, the exact approach is again to refit the model with observation \(i\) omitted and predict \(y_i\). The LOO errors are

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
y_i-\widehat y_{-i}(x_i),
\]

and I would report

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}}
=
\left[
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n
(e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2
\right]^{1/2}.
\]

If \(\theta\) is held fixed at its full-data estimate, define

\[
Q
=
C
-
CF(F^T CF)^{-1}F^T C.
\]

Then

\[
e_i^{\text{LOO}}
=
\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}},
\qquad
\widehat y_{-i}(x_i)
=
y_i-\frac{(Qy)_i}{Q_{ii}}.
\]

Again, numerical values require the missing data file.

## (5) Final model comparison and recommendation rule

I would compare the constant-mean GP and the linear-trend GP using both likelihood-based and prediction-based criteria.

For the constant-mean model,

\[
k_0=1+8+1=10
\]

parameters: \(\mu\), eight \(\theta\)'s, and \(\sigma^2\).

For the linear-trend model,

\[
k_1=3+8+1=12
\]

parameters: \(\beta_0,\beta_1,\beta_2\), eight \(\theta\)'s, and \(\sigma^2\).

I would compute

\[
\operatorname{AIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\psi)+2k,
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{BIC}
=
-2\ell(\widehat\psi)+k\log n.
\]

Because \(n=27\) is small, I would emphasize out-of-sample predictive performance, especially

\[
\operatorname{RMSE}_{\text{LOO}},
\qquad
\operatorname{MAE}_{\text{LOO}},
\qquad
Q^2_{\text{LOO}},
\]

and, if predictive variances are used,

\[
\operatorname{NLPD}
=
\frac1n
\sum_{i=1}^n
\left[
\frac12\log(2\pi \widehat s_{-i}^2)
+
\frac{(e_i^{\text{LOO}})^2}{2\widehat s_{-i}^2}
\right].
\]

A good probabilistic predictor should also have approximately calibrated standardized LOO errors,

\[
z_i
=
\frac{e_i^{\text{LOO}}}{\widehat s_{-i}},
\]

with empirical variance near one and no obvious trend against fitted values.

My model-selection rule would be:

- choose the linear-trend GP if it gives materially smaller LOO RMSE/MAE, larger \(Q^2_{\text{LOO}}\), smaller NLPD, and acceptable AIC/BIC;
- otherwise choose the simpler constant-mean GP.

Without the data, the final model cannot be selected numerically.

## (6) BLUP as a function of \(x_1\) with 95% predictive bands

Let the selected final model have regression vector \(f(x)\), estimated coefficients \(\widehat\beta\), covariance parameter \(\widehat\theta\), and variance estimate \(\widehat\sigma^2\).

To plot the fitted response as a function of \(x_1\), one must hold the other factors fixed. I would typically choose either

1. their nominal center values, or  
2. the estimated optimal values from part (7).

Let

\[
x(t)
=
(t,c_2,c_3,\dots,c_8),
\]

where \(t\) varies over the experimental range of \(x_1\) and \((c_2,\dots,c_8)\) are fixed.

For each grid value \(t\), compute

\[
\widehat m(t)
=
\widehat y\{x(t)\},
\]

and

\[
\widehat s^2(t)
=
\widehat s^2\{x(t)\}.
\]

Then plot

\[
t\mapsto \widehat m(t),
\]

with 95% plug-in predictive bands

\[
\widehat m(t)\pm 1.96\,\widehat s(t).
\]

The plot cannot be produced numerically without the data.

## (7) Optimization of the eight factor settings

For the final fitted model, the predicted mean response has the form

\[
\widehat m(x)
=
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
+
r(x)^T\widehat\alpha,
\]

where

\[
\widehat\alpha
=
R_{\widehat\theta}^{-1}
\{y-F\widehat\beta\}.
\]

The goal is to solve

\[
\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}
=
\arg\min_{x\in \mathcal D}
\widehat m(x),
\]

where \(\mathcal D\) is the feasible region for the eight factors, usually the product of their experimental ranges.

Because \(\widehat m(x)\) is generally nonconvex, I would use a multistart global search followed by local optimization.

For continuous factors, the derivative is available analytically. Let

\[
r_j(x)
=
\exp\left\{
-\sum_{k=1}^8
\widehat\theta_k(x_k-x_{jk})^2
\right\}.
\]

Then

\[
\widehat m(x)
=
f(x)^T\widehat\beta
+
\sum_{j=1}^n
\widehat\alpha_j r_j(x).
\]

For coordinate \(k\),

\[
\frac{\partial \widehat m(x)}{\partial x_k}
=
\frac{\partial f(x)^T\widehat\beta}{\partial x_k}
-
2\widehat\theta_k
\sum_{j=1}^n
\widehat\alpha_j
r_j(x)(x_k-x_{jk}).
\]

For the linear-trend model,

\[
\frac{\partial f(x)^T\widehat\beta}{\partial x_k}
=
\begin{cases}
\widehat\beta_1, & k=1,\\
\widehat\beta_2, & k=6,\\
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

The algorithm would be:

1. Scale all factors to their coded experimental ranges.
2. Generate many starting points in \(\mathcal D\), for example by Latin hypercube or Sobol sampling.
3. Evaluate \(\widehat m(x)\) at all starting points.
4. Keep the best several candidates.
5. From each candidate, run a bounded gradient-based optimizer such as L-BFGS-B using the gradient above.
6. Compare all local minima and choose the one with the smallest predicted gap lift.
7. Report \(\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}}\), \(\widehat m(\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}})\), and the predictive standard error \(\widehat s(\widehat x_{\mathrm{opt}})\).

If some factors are genuinely discrete rather than continuous, I would enumerate their possible levels and run the continuous optimization conditionally on each discrete combination.

The numerical optimum cannot be reported without the missing experiment file.
